Start reading here

Begin with HIA’s own homeland account, which explains the Association’s work in Glacier Bay from a Huna Tlingit perspective. Pair it with the park’s historical account, then turn to HIA’s organizational and environmental pages. The guide keeps this local government distinct from regional institutions and village corporations. Read source annotations for selected pages, dates, perspective and access limits. This is not a complete history or community endorsement.

These are selected starting points. The full annotated collection, source perspectives, inspection limits and remaining research questions follow below. A starting guide is not an exhaustive history or community endorsement.

01

A local government in a longer Huna history

HIA says tribal leaders established the Association in 1939 and describes its Board as the place where decisions, ideas and resolutions are considered. Its account also describes partnerships with other tribal governments and corporations. These relationships do not make those institutions interchangeable, and the Association’s organizational date does not mark the beginning of Huna Tlingit history.

Read the sources [1] Hoonah Indian Association

02

Glacier Bay as homeland

HIA describes Glacier Bay as ancestral homeland and places its collaboration with the National Park Service within that continuing relationship. The park’s account adds institutional context: creation of the national monument in 1925 brought restrictions that curtailed Native activities and strained relations. Reading the two accounts together shows why later cooperative educational, oral-history and return-to-homeland work matters.

Read the sources [2] Hoonah Indian Association [3] National Park Service

03

Building and maintaining a place to gather

HIA explains that work toward Xunaa Shuká Hít, Huna Ancestor’s House, began in the early 1990s and that the partners built and maintain it together. The house was dedicated at Bartlett Cove in August 2016. HIA’s emphasis on a home in Glacier Bay, together with the park’s account of workshops, camps and tribal meetings, offers a public route into the project without retelling ceremonial or clan narratives.

Read the sources [2] Hoonah Indian Association [3] National Park Service

04

Environmental learning as community work

HIA’s environmental-office page describes stewardship and community learning partnerships, including work with the U.S. Forest Service. It provides a contemporary institutional reading route alongside the homeland history. The linked program labels are leads for further study; their effectiveness and present operations have not been evaluated here.

Read the sources [4] Hoonah Indian Association
